import re, pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("source/nilearn/surface/surface.py")
s = p.read_text()

# 1) import stats
old = "from scipy import interpolate, sparse\n"
new = "from scipy import interpolate, sparse, stats\n"
assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)

# 2) insert new sampling function after _interpolation_sampling (before def vol_to_surf)
anchor = "\n\ndef vol_to_surf(\n"
assert s.count(anchor) == 1
func = '''

def _nearest_label_sampling(
    images,
    mesh,
    affine,
    kind="auto",
    radius=3,
    n_points=None,
    mask=None,
    inner_mesh=None,
    depth=None,
):
    """In each image, measure the label at each node of the mesh.

    Like :func:`_nearest_voxel_sampling`, the value measured at each sample
    point is the intensity of the nearest voxel. The difference is the way the
    samples associated with a mesh vertex are combined: instead of averaging
    them, the value that is the most frequent among the samples (the mode) is
    returned.

    Averaging is the correct behaviour when the volume holds a continuous
    quantity, but it is not meaningful for categorical data such as a
    segmentation or an atlas distributed with an anatomical lookup table: an
    average of several labels is generally not one of the labels, so it
    cannot be associated with any row of the table used downstream.

    A 2-d array is returned, where each row corresponds to an image and each
    column to a mesh vertex. Vertices for which every sample falls outside of
    the image, or outside of the mask if one is provided, are assigned
    ``numpy.nan``.
    See documentation of vol_to_surf for details.

    """
    sample_locations = _sample_locations(
        mesh,
        affine,
        kind=kind,
        radius=radius,
        n_points=n_points,
        inner_mesh=inner_mesh,
        depth=depth,
    )
    n_vertices, n_points, _ = sample_locations.shape
    sample_locations = np.asarray(np.round(sample_locations), dtype=int)
    masked = _masked_indices(
        np.vstack(sample_locations), images[0].shape, mask=mask
    ).reshape((n_vertices, n_points))
    image_shape = images[0].shape
    coords = np.rollaxis(sample_locations, -1)
    # Out of bounds samples are clipped so that they can be indexed without
    # error; their values are then discarded through ``masked`` below.
    coords = [
        np.clip(coords[dim], 0, image_shape[dim] - 1) for dim in range(3)
    ]
    texture = np.empty((len(images), n_vertices))
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        # ``stats.mode`` warns for vertices whose samples were all discarded;
        # those vertices are legitimately assigned NaN.
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        for index, img in enumerate(images):
            values = np.asarray(img)[coords[0], coords[1], coords[2]]
            values = values.astype(float)
            values[masked] = np.nan
            modes = stats.mode(values, axis=1, nan_policy="omit")
            texture[index] = np.asarray(modes.mode).ravel()
    return texture
'''
s = s.replace(anchor, func + "\n\ndef vol_to_surf(\n")

# 3) register sampling schemes
old = '''    sampling_schemes = {
        "linear": _interpolation_sampling,
        "nearest": _nearest_voxel_sampling,
    }
'''
new = '''    sampling_schemes = {
        "linear": _interpolation_sampling,
        "nearest": _nearest_voxel_sampling,
        # label-preserving alternatives for categorical volumes, such as an
        # atlas distributed with an anatomical lookup table
        "majority": _nearest_label_sampling,
        "mode": _nearest_label_sampling,
    }
'''
assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)

# 4) docstring interpolation set
old = "    interpolation : {'linear', 'nearest'}, default='linear'\n"
new = "    interpolation : {'linear', 'nearest', 'majority'}, default='linear'\n"
assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)

# 5) docstring interpolation description
old = """        - 'nearest':
            Use the intensity of the nearest voxel.

        For one image, the speed difference is small, 'linear' takes about x1.5
        more time. For many images, 'nearest' scales much better, up to x20
        faster.
"""
new = """        - 'nearest':
            Use the intensity of the nearest voxel.
        - 'majority':
            Use the intensity of the nearest voxel for each sample point and
            then keep the value that is the most frequent among the samples
            of a vertex, instead of averaging them. This is the appropriate
            choice for a categorical volume (for example a segmentation or an
            atlas distributed with an anatomical lookup table), because the
            average of several labels is generally not one of the labels.

        For one image, the speed difference is small, 'linear' takes about x1.5
        more time. For many images, 'nearest' scales much better, up to x20
        faster.
"""
assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)

p.write_text(s)
print("patched")
PY"}

new = '''def _is_label_image(images):
    """Check whether an image stores discrete labels rather than intensities.

    Labelled volumes -- for example the anatomical atlases that are
    distributed together with a lookup table -- store identifiers in integer
    valued voxels. Such values have no numerical meaning, so they must not be
    combined by averaging.
    """
    values = np.asarray(images)
    finite = values[np.isfinite(values)]
    if finite.size == 0:
        return False
    return bool(np.all(finite == np.round(finite)))


def _most_frequent(samples):
    """Most frequent value along the last axis, ignoring ``numpy.nan``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    samples : :obj:`numpy.ndarray`, shape (n_rows, n_samples)
        Sampled values. ``numpy.nan`` entries are treated as missing.

    Returns
    -------
    :obj:`numpy.ndarray`, shape (n_rows,)
        The most frequent value of each row. A row whose samples are all
        missing yields ``numpy.nan``. Ties are broken towards the smallest
        value so that the result is deterministic.

    """
    samples = np.asarray(samples, dtype=float)
    flat = np.sort(samples.reshape(-1, samples.shape[-1]), axis=1)
    n_rows, n_samples = flat.shape
    # NaNs are sorted to the end of each row and, being unequal to
    # themselves, each form a run of their own. They can therefore never win
    # a majority vote against real values.
    new_run = np.ones(flat.shape, dtype=bool)
    new_run[:, 1:] = flat[:, 1:] != flat[:, :-1]
    run_ids = np.cumsum(new_run, axis=1) - 1
    linear_ids = run_ids + np.arange(n_rows)[:, None] * n_samples
    counts = np.bincount(
        linear_ids.ravel(), minlength=n_rows * n_samples
    ).reshape(n_rows, n_samples)
    best_run = counts.argmax(axis=1)
    first_of_best = (run_ids == best_run[:, None]).argmax(axis=1)
    return flat[np.arange(n_rows), first_of_best].reshape(samples.shape[:-1])


def _majority_vote_sampling(
    images,
    mesh,
    affine,
    kind="auto",
    radius=3.0,
    n_points=None,
    mask=None,
    inner_mesh=None,
    depth=None,
):
    """Nearest voxel sampling that preserves labels.

    Every sample point takes the value of the nearest voxel and the values
    collected around a mesh vertex are combined by a majority vote instead of
    being averaged. The value attached to a vertex is therefore always a value
    that actually occurs in the image, which is required when the image is a
    labelled volume looked up in an accompanying table.
    """
    images = np.asarray(images)
    img_shape = images[0].shape
    sample_locations = _sample_locations(
        mesh,
        affine,
        radius=radius,
        kind=kind,
        n_points=n_points,
        inner_mesh=inner_mesh,
        depth=depth,
    )
    sample_locations = np.asarray(np.round(sample_locations), dtype=int)
    n_vertices, n_points, _ = sample_locations.shape
    masked = _masked_indices(
        np.vstack(sample_locations), img_shape, mask=mask
    ).reshape(n_vertices, n_points)
    sample_indices = np.ravel_multi_index(
        np.rollaxis(sample_locations, -1), img_shape, mode="clip"
    )
    kept = ~masked

    texture = np.empty((n_vertices, len(images)))
    for index, volume in enumerate(data):
        samples = np.where(kept, volume[sample_indices], np.nan)

    return texture.T

    mesh,
    affine,
    kind="auto",
    radius=3.0,
    n_points=None,
    mask=None,

    a vertex are combined by a majority vote instead of being averaged, so
    that the projected value is always a valid label. Continuous images keep
    their neighbouring samples averaged.

            mesh,
            affine,
            kind=kind,
            radius=radius,
            n_points=n_points,

    # there is no reasonable value to assign to this vertex.
    # in this case we return NaN for this vertex.
    texture[np.asarray(proj.sum(axis=1) == 0).ravel()] = np.nan

def rand_mats(n):
    ms=[]
    for i in range(n):

                      random.uniform(0.2,0.35), random.uniform(3e3,6e3)))
    return ms

def ref_abd(thetas, thicks, mats):
    z0=-0.5*sum(thicks); zs=[z0]; z=z0
    for t in thicks: z+=t; zs.append(z)
    A=np.zeros((3,3)); B=np.zeros((3,3)); D=np.zeros((3,3))
    tmp=PCOMP(1,mids=list(range(len(thicks))),thicknesses=thicks,thetas=thetas,lam=None)
    for k in range(len(thicks)):
        Qb=tmp.get_Qbar_matrix(mats[k], np.radians(thetas[k]))
        a,b=zs[k],zs[k+1]
        A+=Qb*(b-a); B+=0.5*Qb*(b*b-a*a); D+=(1/3.)*Qb*(b**3-a**3)

    if np.linalg.norm(As[:3,3:])>1e-6: fails+=1; print("NONZERO B",trial)

new='''def _nearest_voxel_sampling(
    images,
    mesh,
    affine,
    kind="auto",
    radius=3.0,
    n_points=None,
    mask=None,
    inner_mesh=None,
    depth=None,
):
    """In each image, measure the intensity at each node of the mesh.

    Image intensity at each sample point is that of the nearest voxel.
    The intensities measured at the sample points around a mesh vertex are
    combined with a majority vote (instead of being averaged) so that the
    value associated to a vertex always belongs to the set of intensities
    present in the image. This keeps the projection meaningful for discrete
    images such as label or atlas volumes, whose intensities must not be
    interpolated or averaged across tissue boundaries.
    A 2-d array is returned, where each row corresponds to an image and each
    column to a mesh vertex.
    See documentation of vol_to_surf for details.

    """
    sample_locations = _sample_locations(
        mesh,
        affine,
        kind=kind,
        radius=radius,
        n_points=n_points,
        inner_mesh=inner_mesh,
        depth=depth,
    )
    n_vertices, n_points_, _ = sample_locations.shape
    img_shape = images[0].shape
    sample_locations = np.asarray(np.round(sample_locations), dtype=int)
    masked = _masked_indices(
        np.vstack(sample_locations), img_shape, mask=mask
    ).reshape(n_vertices, n_points_)
    sample_indices = np.ravel_multi_index(
        np.rollaxis(sample_locations, -1), img_shape, mode="clip"
    )
    data = np.asarray(images).reshape(len(images), -1)
    samples = data[:, sample_indices]
    # ignore sample points that fall outside of the image or of the mask
    samples = np.where(masked[np.newaxis, :, :], np.nan, samples)
    # majority vote over the sample points associated to each mesh vertex
    texture = np.asarray(
        stats.mode(samples, axis=-1, nan_policy="omit").mode
    )
    # if all samples around a mesh vertex are outside the image,
    # there is no reasonable value to assign to this vertex.
    # in this case we return NaN for this vertex.
    texture[:, np.asarray(masked.all(axis=1))] = np.nan
    return texture
